sections.h2: Where is Kootenai County and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Kootenai County sits in the Idaho Panhandle, with Coeur d'Alene as both the county seat and the largest city. It covers 1,316 square miles, of which 1,244 are land and 71 are water, about 5.4 percent (Wikipedia, citing the Census Bureau). The water includes Lake Coeur d'Alene and the southernmost part of Lake Pend Oreille.

Bonner County lies to the north, Shoshone County to the east, Benewah County to the south and Spokane County, Washington, to the west. Parts of the Coeur d'Alene National Forest and the Kaniksu National Forest fall inside the county.

The incorporated cities are Athol, Coeur d'Alene, Dalton Gardens, Fernan Lake Village, Harrison, Hauser, Hayden, Hayden Lake, Huetter, Post Falls, Rathdrum, Spirit Lake, Stateline and Worley. Census-designated places include Conkling Park and Rockford Bay, and unincorporated communities include Bayview, Cataldo, Clarksville, Garwood, Lane and Medimont. A seller's address can sit in a city, on a lake or on rural land, and the rules that apply differ for each.

sections.h2: How did Kootenai County get started?
sections.html:
The Idaho Territorial Legislature created Kootenai County on December 22, 1864, and named it for the Kootenai tribe. A county government was not organized right away because there was little settlement, and the 1864 territorial census counted 81 residents.

The Mullan Road was built through the area in 1859, with a route on the north side of Lake Coeur d'Alene beginning in 1861. Rathdrum was the first of today's incorporated cities to see settlement, starting in 1861, and it became a stagecoach stop and later the county seat. Post Falls was settled in 1871. The Mission of the Sacred Heart at Cataldo finished its mission church by 1855, and that building is described as Idaho's oldest structure.

The older housing near the lake and downtown, and the newer subdivisions spreading toward Post Falls and Rathdrum, come from different eras. Sellers with an older house should expect a buyer's inspection to look closely at roof, wiring and foundation.

sections.h2: How fast has Kootenai County grown?
sections.html:
The county has roughly tripled in size since 1980. The table lists census counts and the Wikipedia 2025 estimate.

Growth between 2000 and 2020 ran at 55.7 percent in the first decade and 23.7 percent in the second. That kind of change affects sellers because more neighborhoods have new construction beside older homes, and because county services and tax districts keep adjusting to a larger base.

sections.h2: What drives the Kootenai County economy?
sections.html:
Health care, schools, hospitality and retail lead the employer list. Idaho Labor Market Information lists the 2024 top employers as Kootenai Health (2,500 to 4,999 employees), then Coeur d'Alene School District, Walmart and Hagadone Hospitality (each 1,000 to 2,499), followed by Silverwood, Kootenai County, Post Falls School District, the Coeur d'Alene Tribe, Lakeland School District and North Idaho College (each 500 to 999) (Kootenai County profile).

Average 2024 employment by industry shows how the work is spread:

  • Education and health services: 17,463
  • Trade, transportation and utilities: 13,560
  • Leisure and hospitality: 11,869
  • Construction: 6,953
  • Professional and business services: 6,710
  • Manufacturing: 5,121

The same profile reports 51,599 workers who lived and worked in the county in 2023 and a county unemployment rate of 4.2 percent in December 2025. Many residents also work across the state line. The profile counts 5,031 jobs held by county residents in Spokane, Washington, 6.5 percent of the total, and 4,008 in Spokane Valley. Coeur d'Alene is 33 miles from Spokane (Idaho Labor Market Information).

sections.h2: What roads, schools and services do Kootenai County sellers point to?
sections.html:
Interstate 90 crosses the county, along with U.S. 95 and state highways 3, 41, 53, 54, 58 and 97. Citylink and Jefferson Lines provide transit service.

Six school districts serve parts of the county:

  • Coeur d'Alene School District 271
  • Kellogg Joint School District 391
  • Kootenai Joint School District 274
  • Lakeland Joint School District 272
  • Plummer-Worley Joint School District 44
  • Post Falls School District 273

North Idaho College draws on the county as its community college taxing district.

sections.h2: What should a Kootenai County seller know about snow, roofs and building rules?
sections.html:
Kootenai County uses its own snow load map and its own amendments to the building code, so a roof is judged against a local standard. The county's residential permit guide lists a minimum frost burial depth for footings of 24 inches and refers builders to the county snow load map. The guide says the county adopted its current construction codes by Ordinance 608, effective January 1, 2020 (Kootenai County permit guide).

For manufactured and mobile homes, the county code allows a legally set home that meets all county and state rules to be relocated without extra proof if it can be verified as built for a roof snow load of at least 30 pounds per square foot (Kootenai County Code, Title 7). If you are selling a manufactured home, gather the data plate and any permits before listing.

Unpermitted work is a common snag in any sale. If you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shop, ask the county building office what permits are on file. A buyer's inspector will ask the same thing.

sections.h2: When are Kootenai County property taxes billed, and what happens if they are late?
sections.html:
Kootenai County mails all tax notices annually by the fourth Monday of November, and taxes are payable on or before December 20 (Treasurer). Failure to receive a bill does not excuse payment, under Idaho Code 63-902(9).

Payment options listed by the treasurer include mail, in person, online by credit card at kcgov.us and phone at 208-446-1005, option 3. Mailed payments count as on time only with a USPS postmark on or before the due date, and the payer covers any transaction fees. Interest on delinquent tax is calculated at one percent per month starting January 1.

The treasurer's FAQ also explains the tax deed track. When real property taxes are three years delinquent, the tax collector sends a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter to the recorded owner. The owner must pay the third year in full to stop the process, and partial payments are applied but do not stop it. An owner who cannot pay may apply to the Board of County Commissioners for hardship relief at 208-446-1600 (Treasurer FAQ). The county also holds a tax deed auction for parcels that reach that stage.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Kootenai County assessment?
sections.html:
The deadline to appeal is the fourth Monday in June, and the county says the only way to file is through the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600 (Assessor appeal page). The Board of Equalization hearing runs like a court and acts in a quasi-judicial capacity (County guide).

Bring evidence that shows the assessed value is wrong, such as a recent appraisal, repair estimates or documentation of damage. Appeals do not pause payment, so plan around the December 20 due date.

The assessor and the treasurer split the work. The assessor handles value and appeals. The treasurer handles bills, payments and delinquencies. A seller who calls the wrong office will lose time.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost in Kootenai County?
sections.html:
Kootenai County's recorder charges $10 for the first page and $3 for each additional page for standard documents, $5.00 per page for surveys, $11.00 for plats, and $1.00 per page for copies of recorded documents (Kootenai County Recorder). State law sets a $15.00 fee for deeds of 30 pages or less. The recorder's office hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding holidays.

When an heir, divorcing spouse or co-owner is involved, record the deed before the sale rather than during closing, so the title company has the full chain in hand.

faqs.q: What is the county seat of Kootenai County?
faqs.a: Coeur d'Alene is the county seat and the largest city in Kootenai County.

faqs.q: When are Kootenai County property tax bills mailed?
faqs.a: The county mails notices annually by the fourth Monday of November, and the tax is payable on or before December 20.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Kootenai County property assessment?
faqs.a: Contact the Board of County Commissioners' office at 208-446-1600 by the fourth Monday in June. The hearing before the Board of Equalization works like a court proceeding.

faqs.q: What happens after three years of unpaid property tax in Kootenai County?
faqs.a: The tax collector sends a Pending Issue of Tax Deed letter to the recorded owner. Paying the third year in full stops the process, and partial payments do not.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Kootenai County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the treasurer at 208-446-1005 for the exact payoff total, then have the title or escrow company pay it from sale proceeds. The county warns that escrow may not pay the treasurer if closing happens before annual tax information is available.
